title: How to Apply Without Getting Scammed
subtitle: Everything you just learned in this course is also a script. This module is how to keep it yours.

blocks.text: Nine modules of real programs, real deadlines and real dollar amounts is exactly the raw material a scammer needs. They do not have to invent a convincing lie about veterans’ benefits or home renovation grants or GST rebates. The real programs already come with real names, real numbers and real urgency built in.
All a scam has to do is borrow the name and change who is asking for your information.

This final module is not about fraud in general. It is about the moment when everything else in this course can be used against you, and the few habits that close that door no matter which program’s name gets borrowed next.
One simple habit can protect every benefit in this course from people who borrow its name.
blocks.detail: Scams copy real programs, real numbers and real deadlines, so knowing the program is not enough on its own.
blocks.extra: Section 02 gives you the one fact that ends most scams.

sections.title: The one fact that ends most of these before they start

blocks.text: No government department in Canada will call, text or email you to demand payment now, threaten arrest, or ask for bank details, a credit card number or your full Social Insurance Number over the phone. That includes the CRA, Veterans Affairs, Natural Resources Canada and Employment and Social Development Canada. This is not a guideline with exceptions. Every one of these departments says so, in writing.

Legitimate government contact looks unglamorous by comparison. A letter by mail. A notice in a secure online portal you logged into yourself. A callback you initiated to a number you looked up independently. None of it arrives with the emotional temperature of a threat, and none of it needs an answer in the next twenty minutes.
Learn that one fact and you have already closed the door on most of what follows in this module. Everything else here is what to do with the fact once you notice the door being tried.

items.title: “If they knew my name, my address and mentioned a real program, it must be legitimate.”
items.text: Scammers do more homework now, and fake caller ID can show a real government number. Knowing your details or a real program name shows someone did research, not who they work for. Check through a channel you control, using a number you looked up yourself, no matter how much the caller seems to know.

sections.title: The shape of it, whichever program’s name gets used

blocks.text: Different scripts, same structure. Recognizing the structure matters more than memorizing any single version, because the version changes every tax season and the structure does not.

items.title: Urgency with a countdown
items.text: Pay in the next thirty minutes or face arrest, account suspension, or losing the benefit. Real programs do not work on a clock that starts when you pick up the phone.

items.title: An unusual payment method
items.text: Gift cards, cryptocurrency, e-transfer to a personal account, or a courier picking up cash. No Canadian government department accepts any of these for a debt, a fee, or to release a benefit.

items.title: A link instead of a login
items.text: An email or text pushing you to click a link to claim a refund or check your account. A real program tells you to log in to an account you already have, the way you normally would.

items.title: A fee to access something free
items.text: Being asked to pay to be told about a grant, or asked for a percentage of an award before you have applied for anything. Every genuine program covered in this course is free to learn about and free to apply for.

items.title: Contact you did not initiate, about something you did not start
items.text: A call about a grant you never applied for, a rebate you never requested, a benefit review you never triggered.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: VERIFY THROUGH A DOOR YOU OPENED YOURSELF

Do not call the number the caller gave you. Do not click the link in the text or email. Instead, look up the department’s number yourself, from a bill you already have or a search you run, and contact them that way. If the contact was real, this costs a few minutes and confirms it. If it was fake, you have closed the door without giving anything up. It works whether the borrowed name is the CRA, Veterans Affairs or a small-business grant. It is the one rule worth memorizing word for word.

sections.title: What a real application actually needs from you

blocks.text: Across the nine modules in this course, real programs asked for ID, income figures, medical forms and bank details for direct deposit. They always did it through a form you opened yourself, on a site you went to on your own. None of them asked for it on a phone call you did not expect.

Your Social Insurance Number needs special care. Some real applications require it. It is also one of the most valuable things a fraudster can get to build a fake identity. Give it only when you started the contact, on an official government site or form. Never give it in reply to an email, text or call you did not expect, however official it sounds. If you are not sure a form needs it, ask the organization first, using a number you looked up yourself.

The paid “helper” showed up in Module 1.5 for small-business grants, and it applies just as much to a veteran’s disability claim, a senior’s renovation grant or a training credit. Anyone charging a fee up front, or a cut of an award, to help you apply for something that is free to apply for is not offering a shortcut. Every free helper named in this course exists so nobody has to pay for this: Service Officers, Community Futures, Small Business Enterprise Centres, employment counsellors and 211.

items.title: “A grant consultant with a professional website and a logo must be legitimate.”
items.text: A website costs little to build, and a logo can be made to look close to an official one without copying it. Neither proves a link to government. The proof that matters is whether the program is on the official page, and whether you can apply to it yourself for free.

sections.title: What to do if you already gave something up

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHAT TO DO IF YOU ALREADY GAVE SOMETHING UP

This happens to careful people. What you do next matters more than the mistake, and speed matters more than shame. If money moved, call your bank or card company right away. Some payments can still be stopped or reversed in the first few hours. If you shared your SIN, bank details or other personal information, contact the department yourself, using a number you look up, and ask about fraud alerts on your account. Report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre whether or not you lost money. They track patterns across many reports, and a report that seems small can be the piece that helps them stop the next one. Nobody who reports has to explain how they were fooled. These scams are built by people who do this for a living, tested on thousands of people and designed to work on careful, smart people under time pressure. Being targeted is not a judgment on you.
Before you respond to anything claiming to be from a government program

items.title: I did not initiate this contact, or I am not certain who initiated it.
I am being asked to act within an unusually short window.
I am being asked to pay by gift card, cryptocurrency, e-transfer to a person, or courier.
I am being asked to click a link rather than log into an account I navigate to myself.
I am being asked for my SIN, full banking details, or a credit card number before I have verified who is asking.
I have not yet looked up the department’s number independently and called it myself.

blocks.text: If more than one of these is true, stop. Hang up, close the message, and verify independently before doing anything else.

sections.title: Harold, the courier, and the phone call he made instead

blocks.text: Harold and the call he made instead
paragraphs: Harold is sixty-eight and lives in Winnipeg. His goal this year is to stay on top of his bills on a fixed income. Then his phone rings on a Tuesday afternoon.

The man says he is with the Canada Revenue Agency. Harold owes several thousand dollars in back taxes from a benefit overpayment, he says, and a warrant will be issued within the hour unless it is paid now. The caller ID shows a number that looks official.

The man is patient, which in hindsight is its own kind of pressure. He stays on the line. He explains exactly what to say to a courier who will come to collect the cash. He keeps saying this is routine and that he is helping Harold avoid something much worse. Harold is not usually anxious about much, but his hands are shaking.

Then Harold remembers one sentence. Months earlier, after a news story about this exact scam, his daughter told him: if anyone calls saying they are the CRA and you owe money, hang up and call the real number yourself.
Harold makes his choice. He tells the man he needs to call him back. He hangs up. Then he dials the number on last year’s Notice of Assessment, not the number the caller gave him.

The real CRA has no record of any debt, any warrant or any call. That afternoon, Harold reports it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. The next weekend, he tells his neighbour the same sentence his daughter told him.
Nothing is lost except twenty minutes and one unpleasant hour.

blocks.text: No government department demands payment now by phone, text or email, or accepts gift cards, cryptocurrency or cash by courier. Check any contact you did not expect through a number you look up yourself, never the one the caller gives you. Nothing in this course requires paying a fee to a third party. Every real program is free to learn about and free to apply for. If something does get through, report it and move fast. Speed matters far more than embarrassment.
Harold kept his savings by hanging up and calling the real CRA number himself.
blocks.detail: The same one sentence can protect you, and anyone you pass it on to.
blocks.extra: Your action this week, in Section 08, starts with saving the real numbers.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Verification Habit

items.title: Save the real phone numbers for the CRA, Service Canada and your provincial benefits office somewhere you will actually find them under pressure, not just in memory.

Tell one person in your life the single rule from this module: verify through a number you looked up yourself, never the one you were given. That sentence is the whole defence, and it is worth passing on the way Harold’s daughter did.
If anything in the past year felt off, a call, a text, a website, report it to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre now. It costs ten minutes and it is never too late to matter.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your verification habit
One rule of thumb: if you are ever unsure mid-call, borrow Harold’s line. “I need to call you back” works on any caller, ends any countdown, and costs you nothing to say.

items.title: Spoofed caller ID
items.text: A trick that shows a fake number on your phone, including real government numbers.

items.title: Phishing
items.text: An email or text made to look official, meant to get you to click a link or share information.

items.title: CAFC
items.text: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre. The national body that collects fraud reports across Canada. The RCMP, the Ontario Provincial Police and the Competition Bureau run it together.

items.title: Verification through an independent channel
items.text: Contacting an organization with a number or address you found yourself, not one given by the person contacting you.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: 1-888-495-8501, or report online at antifraudcentre.ca. Report every incident, even if nothing was lost.
Canada Revenue Agency: 1-800-959-8281 for individuals, to confirm whether a contact claiming to be the CRA is genuine.
Your bank or card issuer: immediately, if money has moved or account details were shared.
Local police, non-emergency line: if you have lost money or believe your identity has been compromised.

blocks.text: If you are in immediate danger or a crime is in progress, call 911.
